article_title: Wilson Reading System®
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Wilson Reading System®. What Works Clearinghouse, Beginning Reading. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Daily 10-part lesson plan in three instructional blocks with built-in review
description: The Wilson Reading System organizes each lesson into "a daily 10-part lesson plan that builds on interaction between the teacher and student," divided into three blocks: parts one through five emphasize word study, parts six through eight emphasize spelling, and parts nine and 10 emphasize fluency and comprehension. The program sequences word-structure instruction from basic word skills to more complex language structure including morphological principles, with reviews reinforcing previous lessons. Lessons run 45–90 minutes in reading classes, small groups, or tutorials.
requirements: A Wilson instructors' manual that helps the teacher prepare the daily lesson
teacher-student interaction as the core of each lesson
constraints: The intensive model of 60–90 minute instruction in small groups or individually is recommended for the most challenged readers
target_learners: striving readers in grade 2 and above
examples: In the reviewed study, a 50-minute lesson was delivered five days a week to groups of three students with various basic reading levels
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Wilson Reading System®. What Works Clearinghouse, Beginning Reading. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/546

article_title: Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency
citation: Qi Zhu, Xiaoming Zhai, Yan Zou, Chunlei Gao. (2026). Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4519-1931
title: WISE Agent: an LLM-based AI feedback tool for sixth-grade essay writing
description: The WISE Agent (Writing Improvement and Smart Evaluation Agent) is an AI feedback tool built on the Coze platform and powered by the DeepSeek Large Language Model, targeting textual logic and perspective biases in student essays. It follows a closed-loop workflow of essay recognition via OCR and image-stitching, tier-based qualitative feedback acting as a "Senior Primary Teacher," and iterative student revision before teacher review. In the study it delivered feedback to 260 sixth-grade students across seven themed essays over three months.
requirements: Handwritten manuscripts undergo standardized OCR and image-stitching; feedback adheres to predefined rubrics and standardized prompts refined through pilot testing (N=120).
constraints: Security is maintained via content anonymization and end-to-end encryption; students revise independently before final teacher review.
examples: Achieving an average correction cycle of 40 seconds, the system signifi- cantly enhances feedback timeliness compared to traditional manual methods.
key_sources: Qi Zhu, Xiaoming Zhai, Yan Zou, Chunlei Gao. (2026). Using AI-Generated Feedback to Improve Critical Thinking and Writing Proficiency. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4519-1931

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: WindowDash: a synthetic food delivery teaching case with 15,000 orders and nine designed patterns
description: WindowDash is a fictional food delivery case for an undergraduate business analytics and visualization assignment, containing 15,000 orders with ten fields including timestamp, ZIP code, service type, cuisine, price, tip, customer rating, and delivery time. Students are asked to find at least five interesting, distinct patterns and submit at least five visualizations with explanations, hypotheses, and a management recommendation. The case includes generation and verification programs, an instructor guide describing nine patterns, an assignment and rubric, and reference visualizations.
requirements: Delivery time is missing for pickup orders because the field does not apply to that service type
constraints: The supplied rubric assigns 30 of the assignment's 50 points to identifying distinct patterns; the Price-Rating Sensitivity pattern rests on only three supporting observations
examples: The Office Lunch Rush pattern requires students to identify the office location, restrict analysis to weekday lunch hours, and compare pickup shares rather than raw counts

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Winne and Hadwin's metacognitive SRL model: four recursive phases and the COPES architecture
description: Winne and Hadwin's model takes a strongly metacognitive, information-processing view of SRL. The review states that "studying is powered by SRL across four linked phases that are open and recursive and are comprehended in a feedback loop": task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting study tactics and strategies, and metacognitively adapting studying. SRL deploys five task facets identified by "the COPES acronym" — Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards — with operations described as SMART (Searching, Monitoring, Assembling, Rehearsing, Translating). Students constantly monitor activities against standards, aligning the model with self-assessment research.
requirements: Scaffolding tools that record trace and log data are used to measure SRL under this model, since no classical questionnaires exist
constraints: The model figure contains no reference to emotions and only an allusion to motivation
examples: Winne's team developed nStudy and gStudy, computer-supported learning environments that scaffold SRL while recording trace data

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: WISE (Web-based Inquiry Science Environment) platform for designing and implementing science inquiry activities
description: WISE is an online platform from the University of California at Berkeley developed along the lines of the knowledge integration approach. It "provides a teacher's portal, including possibilities for classroom management, student assessment, and creating or editing curriculum projects" and a student interface with an inquiry map structuring activities in steps. It supports inquiry steps such as exploring a simulation, brainstorming, constructing an argument, and reflection and self-assessments. Students work in pairs and all teamwork is stored in a database accessible to teachers and researchers for assessment. The authors used the WISE authoring environment to create a new global climate change curriculum project codesigned with science teachers and technology specialists.
requirements: Requires teachers or trained facilitators to support implementation; in this study 46 trained Master's students served as actual teachers during the project
constraints: The curriculum project was designed to be closely tied to the regular Flemish curriculum and integrated with local teaching and learning practices
target_learners: Secondary school students in Grades 9 and 10
target_learning_goals: Science knowledge acquisition about global warming and climate change
examples: A new WISE curriculum project on global warming and climate change was implemented across four 50-min lessons in 19 Flemish secondary classes

article_title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
citation: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle. (2008). A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9035-z
title: Use wikis for collaborative knowledge building because they let many users jointly revise one shared artifact
description: The article argues wikis have special potential for computer-supported collaborative knowledge building because users can not only access but change content online, revising text by "adding, deleting, or changing any parts they want to". In this way large groups jointly create one hypertext, allowing collaborative generation of knowledge, and wikis can be considered to support social constructivist learning in general.
requirements: A wiki accessible to all community members, with revision histories so contributions and restructuring are traceable
constraints: The article focuses on wikis' potential and states possible shortcomings will not take center stage in this analysis
target_learners: members of online communities and learners using wikis for educational purposes
examples: Wikipedia, where users collaboratively develop the world's largest encyclopedia, is applied to make the theoretical analysis concrete

citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Wiki Design Platform with awareness, navigation, communication, and analysis components for online intersubjective space
description: Presented in the issue's first article (Larusson and Alterman), the Wiki Design Platform builds on the wiki's malleable, easy-to-use interface, which the editorial says "is, however, in need of specific kinds of additional functionality for collaborative learning settings." It "provides a suite of awareness, navigation, communication, and analysis components and scaffolds." Two college case studies — HCI design projects and co-blogging about course readings — show different component selections creating an online intersubjective space for different collaboration forms.

constraints: The editorial notes it is not immediately clear which paradigm of shared knowledge the concept of intersubjectivity falls into
target_learning_goals: Collaboration on design projects and co-blogging about course readings
examples: Case study one: student teams collaborating on HCI design projects; case study two: students co-blogging in the wiki about their course readings

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Co-evolution of cognitive and social systems through internalization and externalization in wiki-based learning
description: The article applies a co-evolution account in which individual cognitive systems and collaborative wiki content mutually shape each other. Learners internalize wiki information through internal assimilation or accommodation processes, changing their own knowledge, and externalize it by adding content or restructuring wiki sections. This framework explains why cognitive and behavioral processes are closely intertwined in wiki-based learning.
requirements: Beneficial learning requires encountering information that contrasts with learners' original assumptions.
constraints: Not all types of interaction have the same beneficial effects; simple participation does not guarantee valuable qualitative cognition in wiki collaboration.
target_learners: Wiki users in collaborative learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: Individual knowledge acquisition through wiki interaction
examples: The article connects Piaget's cognitive conflict to wiki collaboration: encountering contrasting viewpoints triggers internal assimilation/accommodation for individual learning and external assimilation/accommodation for wiki restructuring.

article_title: Using multiple, contextualized data sources to measure learners’ perceptions of their self-regulated learning
citation: McCardle, L. (2015). Self-regulated learning in and across sport and academic domains [Doctoral dissertation, University of Victoria]. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9132-0
title: Winne and Hadwin's (1998) COPES model of SRL as a framework for researching SRL transfer across domains
description: The dissertation adopts Winne and Hadwin's (1998) four-phase model with the COPES architecture (conditions, operations, products, evaluations, standards) as its theoretical framework. SRL is defined as "learners' active engagement of processes to control and adapt cognition, behaviour, and motivation/affect to reach self-set goals". The model is recursive with weakly sequenced phases, allocates a central role to metacognitive monitoring and control within each phase, and its inclusion of conditions allows learning to be treated as situated. The author recommends it "serve as a framework for researching SRL transfer with a focus on conditions" because it describes regulatory processes that are similar across contexts even when tactics differ.
requirements: Research on SRL transfer should attend to conditions surrounding learning, per the model's COPES architecture
constraints: The author argues current theories of transfer have little to say about SRL because SRL is a dynamic process rather than static knowledge
target_learning_goals: transfer of regulatory processes between sport and academics
examples: The dissertation uses the model to argue that both students and athletes define tasks, set goals, monitor and evaluate learning, and make changes when progress goes awry, even though tactics differ across contexts

article_title: Primary school students’ awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy
citation: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907
title: Analyze accuracy awareness at the within-student level using multiple measurement points
description: The article argues that true awareness of judgment accuracy requires analyzing whether an individual student's increase in judgment accuracy is accompanied by an increase in confidence, which demands multiple measurements per student. Between-student analyses answer a different question — whether students with higher accuracy are generally more confident — and "could have concluded that students showed awareness of their monitoring and regulation accuracy on the division task" even though within-student analyses showed no awareness. Researchers studying accuracy awareness should regress SOJs on judgment accuracy at the day (within-student) level with group-mean centering.
requirements: At least two measurement points per student (e.g., parallel task versions on different days)
Multilevel regression with judgment accuracy centered at the group mean for within-student effects
constraints: Between-student and within-student analyses answer different questions and may lead to different conclusions about the same data
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of monitoring and regulation accuracy awareness
examples: The authors regressed SOJ-m/SOJ-r on monitoring/regulation accuracy at the day level in three-level multilevel models (day, student, class) using Mplus with MLR estimation

article_title: The learning of delinquent adolescent girls as shown by a substitution test.
citation: Baldwin, B. T. (1913). The learning of delinquent adolescent girls as shown by a substitution test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(6), 317-332.
title: Wig-wag code substitution test with typewriter-layout keyboard

The task was administered for sixteen five-minute practice periods and yielded counts of substitutions and errors per girl.

article_title: Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy "transfer"?
citation: W. H. Winch. (1910). Accuracy in school children. Does improvement in numerical accuracy 'transfer'? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Winch+accuracy+school+children
title: Value numerical accuracy for its practical worth, not as a means of indirectly training arithmetical reasoning
description: From the four experiments the author draws a pedagogical recommendation: pending more conclusive experiments, teachers should pursue computational accuracy for its own practical value rather than expecting it to train reasoning indirectly. He writes that "numerical accuracy should be sought for because it is valuable in actual life, and not because we can feel con- fident that an improvement in it will transfer to accuracy of arithmetical reasoning." This directly follows from the null and irregular transfer findings across the schools.
requirements: Indirect training of reasoning through computation practice should not be relied on until further experiments establish transfer quantitatively
constraints: The author states the recommendation holds pending more conclusive experiments, given the irregularity of the results
examples: In all four schools, matched groups were formed on preliminary reasoning tests, one group practised rule sums while the other did drawing, history or English composition, and final reasoning tests compared the groups.

article_title: How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System?
citation: Taub, M., & Azevedo, R. (2019). How Does Prior Knowledge Influence Eye Fixations and Sequences of Cognitive and Metacognitive SRL Processes during Learning with an Intelligent Tutoring System? Int J Artif Intell Educ (2019) 29:1-28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0165-4
title: Winne and Hadwin's information processing theory of SRL: four cyclical phases shaped by cognitive conditions such as prior knowledge
description: The article adopts Winne & Hadwin's information processing theory of SRL, in which "learning occurs through a series of four cyclical phases, where SRL is an event that unfolds over time". The phases are task understanding, goal setting and planning, enacting learning strategies, and adapting goals, plans, and strategies; they are cyclical, not necessarily sequential, and can run simultaneously. The model also posits cognitive conditions, including prior domain knowledge, that impact how students progress through the phases. The authors use it to frame their investigation of prior knowledge effects on SRL during MetaTutor learning.

constraints: Phases are cyclical and not necessarily sequential; students may engage multiple phases simultaneously
target_learners: college students learning complex science topics
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during learning with intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The study tested the model's claim that prior domain knowledge, a cognitive condition, impacts SRL phases during learning with MetaTutor.

title: Winne and Hadwin's four-phase cognitive information processing model of SRL
description: Winne and Hadwin's (2013) model conceptualizes SRL as involving four loosely sequential phases: task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting tactics and strategies, and adaptation. description: The article's closing recommendation is that learning environment design should draw on the full breadth of the framework rather than isolated principles. title: Window of Interaction framework: eight dimensions defining the interactive potential of an artifact
description: The Window of Interaction (WoI) framework, drawn from HCI by Janlert and Stolterman, provides "an analytical and descriptive approach to understanding how technology is designed to foster interaction." It analyzes interactivity as a property of designed artifacts rather than user experience, rating eight dimensions from low to high: agency, independence, receptivity, predictability, freedom of action, pace/time, attention demand, and awareness level. constraints: The framework "does not offer quantifiable measurements akin to hard sciences but rather is subject to individual judgments that are subjective by nature"

examples: The authors operationalized five WoI dimensions into interview questions and artifact-analysis rubrics (Table 1), rating each of 19 learning objects low/medium/high on each dimension

citation: Ross E. O'Hara, Betsy Sparrow. (2019). A Summer Nudge Campaign to Motivate Community College STEM Students to Reenroll. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419875715
title: Wise interventions targeting psychosocial barriers: social belonging, values affirmation, and self-transcendent purpose for learning
description: The article frames its intervention within "wise interventions," programs "designed to create behavior changes that endure past the end of treatment" that target the attitude, belief, or mindset underlying a maladaptive behavior rather than the behavior itself, triggering a recursive process in which the environment reinforces new beliefs. Three approaches are central: social belonging (normalizing struggle to dissociate social identities from college obstacles), values affirmation (reestablishing self-worth during identity threat), and self-transcendent purpose for learning (connecting learning to helping others and making a difference). The summer nudges combined these to address psychosocial barriers to community college STEM persistence.
requirements: Delivery must target the underlying cognition (attitude, belief, or mindset) rather than the maladaptive behavior directly
constraints: The article notes the intervention took an omnibus approach combining several techniques, so the mechanisms were not isolated
The authors note cultural mismatch may be felt less strongly at 2-year colleges, possibly dampening effects on the general student population
target_learners: students at risk of withdrawal from college
examples: The intervention delivered two nudges per week via text message from June 28 to August 18, 2017, combining social belonging, values affirmation, and self-transcendent purpose messages, with alternative nudges diagnosing barriers for unenrolled students

examples: The author used the framework to develop a fidelity measure in an RCT of the Data Modeling middle school statistics curriculum, addressing four questions about constructs, items, outcomes, and measurement modeling.

The platform's Recent Activity mode also recorded each user's activity, which the teacher used to complete collaboration rubrics.
requirements: Students work at computers with internet connection (workstations), as the experimental group did
constraints: The article notes implementation depends on familiarizing trainers and trainees with technology, the degree of planning, the number of students and the teachers' ability to stimulate students (citing prior literature)
target_learners: second-grade General Lyceum students (16-17 years old)
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills and attitudes in Modern Greek Literature
examples: The experimental group used wiki pbworks workstations during a thirteen-hour Literature intervention covering three literary texts, while the control group was taught cooperatively without computers

article_title: A Feasibility Study of Task-Based Teaching of College English Writing in Chinese EFL Context
citation: Linying Cao. (2012). A Feasibility Study of Task-based Teaching of College English Writing in Chinese EFL Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p80
title: Jane Willis' framework for task-based learning as a writing pedagogy
description: Willis' framework for task-based learning organizes instruction into three components: "the ‘pre-task’, ‘task cycle’ and ‘language focus’ components". Applied to writing, the end product is introduced orally or through reading in the pre-task phase, discussed at the task stage, drafted collaboratively at planning, and finalized for the report stage. The article uses this framework as the experimental treatment, arguing it attends to both fluency during the task cycle and accuracy in the language-focus phase.
requirements: A written task is set with useful words, phrases and background knowledge highlighted before the task cycle begins
Learners discuss, plan, draft, exchange drafts for peer suggestions, redraft, and report to the class audience
constraints: Willis does not describe in detail how to employ the framework to organize writing classroom activities, so the writing-specific procedure is the author's reconstruction
target_learners: graduate students in English writing courses
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy and fluency in meaning conveyance
examples: In the six-week experiment, the experimental class composed four teacher-guided pieces under this framework plus uncontrolled pretest and posttest pieces
key_sources: Linying Cao. (2012). A Feasibility Study of Task-based Teaching of College English Writing in Chinese EFL Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p80

article_title: An Analysis of the Application of Wikipedia Corpus on the Lexical Learning in the Second Language Acquisition
citation: Jing Shi. (2015). An Analysis of the Application of Wikipedia Corpus on the Lexical Learning in the Second Language Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 8(8). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n8p171
title: Wikipedia Corpus (Mark Davis)
description: The Wikipedia Corpus is a free online corpus tool compiled and designed by Mark Davis, containing "the full text of the English version of Wikipedia, 1.9 billion words in more than 4.4 million articles." It allows users to search by word, phrase, part of speech, and synonyms, find collocates, and view re-sortable concordance lines in KWIC format. The article uses it as the intervention tool in the experimental group's lexical learning activities.
requirements: Users need only a short, simple orientation; the interface is described as easy to handle and similar to a familiar search engine.
constraints: The article notes the tool was less effective for low-level learners who found the corpus-based method too challenging.
target_learners: First-year university English majors in mainland China
target_learning_goals: Second language (English) lexical acquisition, including word meaning, part of speech, collocations, and commonly used expressions
examples: Students typed in the word "finance", displayed concordance lines in KWIC format, identified collocations, and discussed their findings in groups.

article_title: Assessing the predictive validity of expectancy theory for academic performance.
citation: Permzadian, V., & Shen, T. (2024). Assessing the predictive validity of expectancy theory for academic performance. BMC Psychology, 12. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01935-y
title: Test motivation constructs with within-person designs and theory-congruent measurement when assessing their validity
description: The article argues that inconsistent prior results for expectancy theory stem partly from methodological deviations: between-person designs when Vroom conceived motivation as within-person, researcher-provided rather than participant-generated second-level outcomes, and valence scales with only positive anchors. Assessing motivation–performance links using within-person multilevel modeling, participant-generated outcomes, and bidirectional scales enabled a more appropriate test that revealed the simplified force model's validity.
requirements: Participants must be able to generate their own second-level outcomes rather than choose from a researcher-provided list
Course-level observations must be nested within persons and analyzed with multilevel modeling
Measurement must match the theory's original operationalizations (e.g., expectancy as probability of goal success given effort)
constraints: The article attributes prior weak support partly to these methodological issues but cannot definitively show they explain all inconsistency
examples: The study let participants list up to seven anticipated outcomes of an A grade per course, both positive and negative, and used 0-100% probability scales for expectancy
key_sources: Permzadian, V., & Shen, T. (2024). Assessing the predictive validity of expectancy theory for academic performance. BMC Psychology, 12. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-024-01935-y

article_title: Student perspectives of simulated learning to improve their dysphagia management.
citation: Adams, S.N., Kater, K-A., & Seedat, J. (2024). Student perspectives of simulated learning to improve their dysphagia management. South African Journal of Communication Disorders, 71(1), a1060. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajcd.v71i1.1060
title: Wits dysphagia simulation laboratory using the HAL S3201 mannequin with programmed stroke and TBI scenarios
description: The simulated learning environment at the University of the Witwatersrand centres on "the advanced HAL® S3201 Multipurpose Patient Simulator from Gaumard Scientific", programmed with vital signs, orientation and language screener responses, and overt dysphagia signs such as coughing, choking and oxygen saturation changes indicating aspiration. Students completed two timed scenarios (15 and 10 minutes) — a middle cerebral artery stroke and a traumatic brain injury case — performing file review, communication, dysphagia assessment and feedback tasks under researcher supervision, with a dialogic feedback process after tasks.
requirements: Facilitators completed a 1-day training programme on teaching using simulation before running the activities
constraints: The mannequin did not display physical characteristics such as facial weakness or drooling; these were described to the student by the facilitator
examples: Scenario 2 programmed silent aspiration with semi-solids, with oxygen saturation dropping and respiratory rate increasing
key_sources: Adams, S.N., Kater, K-A., & Seedat, J. (2024). Student perspectives of simulated learning to improve their dysphagia management. South African Journal of Communication Disorders, 71(1), a1060. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajcd.v71i1.1060

article_title: Self-directed learning in post-graduate medical education: Self-judgement and supervisor judgement of competence development in Austrian nine-month basic training.
citation: Khünl-Brady-Ertl Gudrun, Oeser Reinhard, Seemann-Hlawati Barbara, Varga Katja, Wagner-Menghin Michaela. (2024). Self-directed learning in post-graduate medical education: Self-judgement and supervisor judgement of competence development in Austrian nine-month basic training. GMS Journal for Medical Education 41(4): Doc42. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2024-41/zma001697.shtml
title: WIGEV LOGBUCH Basisausbildung — a rotation-structured basic-training logbook with self- and supervisor-judgement scales and reflection tasks
description: The "LOGBUCH Basisausbildung" is the logbook accompanying Austrian basic training at the Vienna Healthcare Group. It groups the ÖÄK's 81 learning objectives into three competence levels ("knowledge", "experience" and "proficiency"), pairs them with 10-point self- and supervisor-judgement percentage scales, and adds structured and free reflection tasks. Junior physicians maintain it independently across three three-month department rotations, using it in mid-term and final evaluations to collect supervisor feedback.
requirements: Requires junior physicians to document continuously and independently across the whole training period, with education officers explaining its use at introduction
constraints: The study notes junior physicians may not document subjective learning needs for fear of negative consequences, mitigated by procedural precautions
target_learners: junior physicians in postgraduate basic medical training
target_learning_goals: mastering ÖÄK-defined basic clinical learning objectives at knowledge, experience and proficiency levels
examples: In the study, 147 logbooks from the 2016–2018 training cohorts of three WIGEV clinics were analysed at months 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9

article_title: How interactions between ADHD and schools affect educational achievement: a family-based genetically sensitive study.
citation: Cheesman Rosa, Eilertsen Espen M., Ayorech Ziada, Borgen Nicolai T., Andreassen Ole A., Larsson Henrik, Zachrisson Henrik, Torvik Fartein A., Ystrom Eivind. (2022). How interactions between ADHD and schools affect educational achievement: a family‐based genetically sensitive study. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, and Allied Disciplines. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.13656
title: A within-family multilevel framework for investigating gene–environment interactions in school contexts
description: The article introduces an analytic framework combining multilevel random-slope models with within-family polygenic score adjustment to detect latent moderation of genetic effects by environments. The authors state: "We have developed a robust framework to investigate gene–environment interactions based on multilevel modelling of within‐family data that could be used in future studies." It keeps the researcher agnostic to which specific environmental factors moderate the genetic effect.
requirements: Requires parent–offspring genotype trios and linked environmental and outcome registers with identifiers for the grouping context
constraints: Active gene–environment correlation is not adjusted for where children can select their own school context
target_learners: School-age children with elevated ADHD symptoms or genetic risk
target_learning_goals: Educational achievement in standardised national tests
examples: Applied in the study to estimate between-school variation in within-family ADHD-PGS effects on Norwegian national test scores across 2,579 schools.

article_title: Comparing computer-assisted learning activities for learning clinical neuroscience: a randomized control trial.
citation: Rajan Kiran, Pandit Anand S. (2022). Comparing computer-assisted learning activities for learning clinical neuroscience: a randomized control trial. BMC Medical Education 22:522. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03578-2
title: Wikipedia-style webpage control activity with identical content but no interactivity
description: A Wikipedia-style page created on Wikidot.com as the control computer-assisted learning activity. Its content was "identical to the eModule: including use of the same images, but without interactivity or clinical cases", and its design followed the structure of medical articles on Wikipedia. Creation took an estimated 10 h, compared with roughly 60 h for the eModule, illustrating the sharply different cost of the two delivery formats.
requirements: Content must match the interactive alternative to isolate the effect of interactivity
constraints: Lacks interactivity, complex 3D graphics, virtual cases and reliable peer review relative to eModules
target_learners: UK medical students on clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Learning stroke and cerebrovascular anatomy content equivalent to the eModule
examples: The Wiki page used the same images as the eModule and factual Wikipedia-like delivery and structure

article_title: Communication skills training and the conceptual structure of empathy among medical students.
citation: Son Daisuke, Shimizu Ikuo, Ishikawa Hirono, Aomatsu Muneyoshi, Leppink Jimmie. (2018). Communication skills training and the conceptual structure of empathy among medical students. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-018-0431-z
title: Newly developed three-item willingness to show empathic behaviour scale
description: The authors developed a three-item scale (items 21-23, e.g., "I will show empathic behaviour to patients when I see their distress") to measure students' willingness to show empathic behaviour in the context of medical interviewing training and the OSCE. Confirmatory factor analysis showed high standardized loadings (0.941-0.986), which the authors say indicate "the attempt to create a unidimensional willingness to show empathic behaviour scale has succeeded". Face validity was acquired from tutors' and students' experiences and comments.
requirements: Face validation from tutors and students in the training context
constraints: The items did not undergo validation additional to the establishment of face validity
The authors note the items could be developed further and adapted for different contexts
target_learning_goals: measuring willingness to show empathic behaviour
examples: Administered twice with the Jefferson Scale of Empathy after communication skills training in three Japanese universities

article_title: Laser visual guidance versus two-dimensional vision in laparoscopy: a randomized trial.
citation: Sørensen Stine Maya Dreier, Mahmood Oria, Konge Lars, Thinggaard Ebbe, Bjerrum Flemming. (2016). Laser visual guidance versus two-dimensional vision in laparoscopy: a randomized trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-016-4937-3
title: Wickens Multiple Resource Theory as the rationale for why visual depth aids may improve laparoscopic performance
description: The authors base their expectation that LVG will help on Wickens Multiple Resource Theory, which "postulates that humans have multiple cognitive resources that can be accessed simultaneously". Because a single cognitive resource has limited processing capacity, performing tasks that draw on the same resource — operating while compensating for lost depth perception — can impair performance. LVG "reintroduces binocular depth cues", which should theoretically make movements faster and more precise.
requirements: Applies when tasks compete for a single limited cognitive resource
constraints: The authors present it as a theoretical rationale; the trial's workload and performance data did not confirm the predicted benefit
examples: Used to explain why a depth-restoring visual aid was expected to reduce time and errors in laparoscopy

article_title: Effectiveness of an interactive website aimed at empowerment of disability benefit claimants: results of a pragmatic randomized controlled trial.
citation: Samoocha D, Snels IAK, Bruinvels DJ, Anema JR, van der Beek AJ. (2011). Effectiveness of an Interactive Website Aimed at Empowerment of Disability Benefit Claimants: Results of a Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Occupational Rehabilitation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10926-010-9283-z
title: www.wiagesprek.nl — interactive empowerment website with five preparation modules for disability claimants
description: A web-based intervention giving disability claimants access to "Five interactive lessons or 'modules'" that each "prepared participants step-by-step for their meeting with the insurance physician". Module 1 (~20 min) explained Dutch WIA legislation with an interactive quiz; module 2 (~20 min) had claimants fill out a medical record and keep an online diary; module 3 (~15 min) showed videos of patient–physician interaction to teach active participation; module 4 (~15 min) discussed expectations with the "WIA meter" self-awareness tool; module 5 (~5 min) summarized the modules and six preparation tips. The site also offered general information and a claimant forum.
requirements: Participants needed an email address and logon credentials (username and password) to access the website
Modules were completed at the participant's own pace in approximately one week before the disability assessment
constraints: The trial found the intervention not effective in increasing empowerment or coping, and it had a significant adverse effect on perceived procedural justice
The authors state serious considerations should be made before implementing it in daily practice, though it could serve as a useful information source
target_learners: Disability benefit claimants applying for a work disability pension after 104 weeks of sickness absence
target_learning_goals: Increase knowledge of social security legislation and assessment procedures
Increase self-awareness, expectations, self-efficacy, and active participation in the assessment interview
examples: In the pragmatic RCT, 123 claimants were given access to the website; 33% never logged on and 22% finished all five modules
